title: The Sages Prescribe Balarama's Penance
story:
At Naimisha the grove had gone quiet. The suta Romaharshana lay where he had fallen, in the very enclosure where he had been reciting the ancient tales, and the cry the sages had raised still hung in the air like smoke: brahma-hatya — the slaying of a brahmana, a man of the priestly order. And the man who had struck the blow stood before them, waiting.

He was Balarama — Krishna's elder brother, who had come to the Naimisha forest as a pilgrim and been welcomed to the sages' great sacrifice, a rite that ran on season after season. When he had arrived among them, Romaharshana alone had remained seated, the one man in all that assembly who had not risen to greet him, and the answer had been terrible and swift: one blade of kusha grass, and the voice that had filled the grove fell silent forever. The suta had been dear to the sages, a voice that had carried the ancient lore across the years. Now the heaviest sin of the old law lay on Balarama, and every man in that grove knew its weight, for the killing of a brahmana is the sin that even the gods are said to fear.

The sages did not rage at him. They had cried out at the deed; now they drew together and spoke of atonement, as elders speak to one who has failed, and what they prescribed was no small thing. They told him of the demon Balvala, son of Ilvala, who had plagued their sacrifice for as long as any of them could remember. At every parvan — at the close of each cycle of rites, at the time of the new moon and of the full — the demon came down from the sky and rained filth and impurity upon the fire, defiling what years of penance had made pure, so that the sacrifice had to be begun again from the first offering. Year after year their rites had been broken by him, and they had been powerless to stop it. "Slay that cruel one," the sages said, "and that shall be the first part of your penance." Then they spoke the second part: for twelve months Balarama must wander through all of Bharatavarsha, the sacred land, bathing at its holy fords and washing the stain from himself in its waters, until the turning of the year had cleansed him.

Balarama heard the whole of it without flinching. He might have argued that the suta had dishonored the sages first, that respect had been broken before his blade was drawn; he said none of it. The killing had been his; the cleansing would be his as well. He stood before the sages and accepted — the slaying of the demon and the year of wandering both — and the old text is careful to say that he undertook the expiation for the benefit of the world, not only for himself.

So the penance was set, and the grove settled back toward its long rite with a new understanding: the man who had broken the silence of Naimisha would answer for it at the next parvan, when Balvala came again to rain his filth upon the fire. The sages returned to their seats. Balarama remained among them, watching the flame that the demon had defiled so many times, waiting for the season of his atonement to begin.
reflection: The sages answer bloodshed not with punishment but with a task: the sin is to be washed out in action — by facing the demon who has plagued their rites, and by a year of walking the sacred land. Balarama accepts without defense or argument, and the old text says he did it for the benefit of the world; the burden, once accepted, turns outward and becomes service.
next_story_tease: At the next parvan the demon would come again to defile the fire — and Balarama's penance would meet him.
hero_scene: In the lamplit sacrificial enclosure of the Naimisha forest, the sages sit in a wide circle about their fire, their hands raised in instruction, while Balarama stands before them in acceptance — the fallen suta lying still beyond the firelight, a blade of kusha grass beside him.
